questions.title: How would you architect an enterprise web application on AWS?
questions.quick: I would start from requirements: availability, traffic shape, security, team capacity and budget. A typical web design puts a load balancer in front of containerised services on ECS or EC2 across multiple Availability Zones, uses RDS for relational data, S3 for objects, IAM roles for access and CloudWatch for monitoring, all delivered through a CI/CD pipeline. Where it fits, I would add API Gateway and Lambda for event-driven pieces. I would keep the data tier in private subnets and treat the final shape as a set of trade-offs, not a template.
questions.revision: Requirements first; then load balancer, containers across AZs, managed database, object storage, IAM, monitoring and CI/CD. Add serverless where events fit. Justify every choice by availability, security, cost and team capacity.
questions.detailed:
There is no single correct enterprise architecture. A defensible answer starts with requirements (availability target, traffic profile, data sensitivity, compliance, team skills, budget) and then assembles building blocks that satisfy them.

{{diagram:ref}}

## Typical layers
| Layer | Common choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Edge | CDN, DNS, WAF | Caching, TLS, filtering of abusive traffic |
| Entry | Application Load Balancer (or API Gateway) | Health-checked routing across zones |
| Compute | ECS/Fargate, EC2 Auto Scaling, or Lambda | Match the workload shape |
| Data | RDS or Aurora (Multi-AZ), S3, optional cache | Managed backups and failover |
| Identity | IAM roles, least privilege | No long-lived keys in code |
| Operations | CloudWatch, tracing, CI/CD | Visibility and repeatable releases |

## Design decisions to call out
- **Availability**: spread compute across at least two Availability Zones; use a Multi-AZ database. Multi-Region is a separate, costlier decision driven by recovery objectives.
- **Security**: public subnets only for load balancers; app and database tiers private; security groups scoped by source; secrets in a managed secret store; encryption at rest and in transit.
- **Scaling**: stateless services scale horizontally; keep session and file state outside the instance.
- **Operability**: infrastructure as code, tagging, alarms tied to user-facing symptoms.
- **Cost**: right-size, and prefer managed services when they remove operational work the team cannot afford to do well.

## Common mistakes
- Drawing a diagram before stating the non-functional requirements.
- Putting databases in public subnets or sharing one broad IAM role across services.
- Choosing Kubernetes or multi-Region "just in case" for a modest workload.
- Forgetting deployment, monitoring and backup, which are part of the architecture.

## Example (hypothetical)
An internal order-management portal expecting steady weekday traffic: ALB, two containerised services on Fargate in two zones, a Multi-AZ PostgreSQL instance, S3 for documents, a queue plus Lambda for nightly report generation, and a pipeline that deploys with automatic rollback.

diagrams.title: Reference web architecture
diagrams.alt: Users reach a CDN and WAF, then an application load balancer. The balancer routes to containerised services in private subnets. Services use a relational database, object storage and a queue feeding a Lambda function, and emit telemetry to CloudWatch.

followUps: How would you make this survive the loss of an Availability Zone?
Where would you place secrets and how would services read them?
What changes if the system must meet a strict Region-level recovery objective?

questions.title: ECS versus Lambda: how do you choose?
questions.quick: I would choose ECS for long-running, containerised services where I need control over the runtime, dependencies and service lifecycle, such as persistent APIs and background workers. I would choose Lambda for event-driven, short-lived work like scheduled jobs, queue or file processing and lightweight integrations, where managed scaling is valuable. I would compare execution limits, concurrency behaviour, cold-start latency, networking needs, cost at the expected load and how much operations work the team can carry. Often a system uses both.
questions.revision: ECS for long-running containerised services needing runtime control; Lambda for short, event-driven work with managed scaling. Compare limits, latency, concurrency, networking, cost and operational load.
questions.detailed:
Both run application code without you managing physical servers, but they differ in execution model. **ECS** (usually with Fargate or EC2 capacity) runs containers as long-lived tasks you define. **Lambda** runs a function per event, scaling the number of concurrent executions automatically.

## Comparison
| Aspect | ECS (Fargate/EC2) | Lambda |
|---|---|---|
| Unit | Container task or service | Function invocation |
| Duration | Long-running | Bounded per invocation (check current limit) |
| Scaling | Service auto scaling on metrics, takes minutes | Per-event, very fast, bounded by concurrency quotas |
| Runtime control | Any image, any process model | Supported runtimes or container image within limits |
| Latency | Warm and steady | Possible cold starts on new environments |
| Cost shape | Pay for provisioned task time | Pay per request and duration; idle costs near zero |
| Ops effort | Images, task sizing, deployments | Packaging, timeouts, concurrency settings |

## Rules of thumb
- Persistent HTTP APIs with steady traffic, WebSockets, or workers that hold connections: **ECS**.
- Spiky or infrequent event handling (S3 uploads, queue messages, schedules, webhooks): **Lambda**.
- Heavy CPU, large memory or long jobs beyond function limits: **ECS** or a batch service.
- Very high steady throughput: compare costs; always-on containers can be cheaper than per-invocation billing.

## Trade-offs and mistakes
- Treating Lambda as a free lunch: downstream databases can be overwhelmed by scaled-out concurrency; use reserved concurrency or a connection proxy.
- Running a rarely used batch job on an always-on service and paying for idle capacity.
- Ignoring local development, observability and testing differences between the two models.
- Splitting a simple app into dozens of functions and creating an operational maze.

## Example (hypothetical)
A document portal runs its REST API as an ECS service behind a load balancer. When a file lands in S3, a Lambda function extracts metadata, and a scheduled Lambda emails a daily summary. Each piece uses the model that suits its load.
followUps: How do cold starts affect a user-facing API, and what can you do about them?
How would you protect a database from a burst of Lambda concurrency?
When is EC2 launch type preferable to Fargate?

questions.title: What is the purpose of an API Gateway, and what does it not do?
questions.quick: An API Gateway is a controlled entry point in front of backend APIs. I would use it for routing to different backends, integrating authentication, throttling, request validation, caching where suitable and collecting access metrics. It simplifies what clients need to know about the backends. But I would not treat it as a substitute for application-level authorization, business validation or secure service-to-service communication. The backend still has to check that this caller may act on this resource, and internal calls still need their own authentication.
questions.revision: A gateway centralises routing, auth integration, throttling, validation and metrics at the edge. It never replaces backend authorization, business rules or internal service security.
questions.detailed:
An API gateway is a managed front door for APIs. Clients talk to one stable endpoint; the gateway applies cross-cutting policy and forwards requests to the right backend (containers, functions, or other HTTP services).

## What it typically provides
- **Routing**: map paths and methods to different backends, hiding internal topology.
- **Authentication integration**: validate tokens (for example JWTs from an identity provider) or API keys before the request reaches the backend.
- **Throttling and quotas**: protect backends from abusive or runaway clients and enforce usage plans.
- **Request validation and transformation**: reject malformed payloads early; adapt formats where needed.
- **Observability**: central access logs, latency and error metrics.
- **Versioning and staging**: expose stages or versions without changing clients.

## What it does not do
| Concern | Still your responsibility |
|---|---|
| Authorization of a specific resource | Backend checks the caller owns or may access it |
| Business validation | Domain rules, invariants, data consistency |
| Service-to-service security | Mutual TLS, signed requests or IAM between internal services |
| Reliability of the backend | Timeouts, retries, idempotency, capacity |

## Trade-offs
- It is another component with its own latency, limits and cost; check the product's current quotas and payload limits.
- Heavy logic placed in gateway mappings becomes hard to test and version.
- A single gateway can become a shared bottleneck or ownership problem across teams; consider per-domain gateways.
- On AWS, an application load balancer is a simpler choice when you only need layer 7 routing to containers and no gateway features.

## Common mistakes
- Assuming "the gateway authenticated the user" means the backend can skip authorization.
- Leaving backends reachable directly from the internet, bypassing the gateway.
- Not setting sensible throttles and timeouts.

## Example (hypothetical)
A mobile app calls /orders and /profile on one hostname. The gateway validates the token, throttles per client, routes /orders to an order service and /profile to another. The order service still verifies that the order belongs to the authenticated user.
followUps: How does an API gateway differ from a load balancer?
Where should authorization be enforced in a microservice system?
How would you prevent clients from bypassing the gateway?

questions.title: How do you design a CI/CD pipeline?
questions.quick: I would build the pipeline so every change is reproducible and verified before it reaches users. Commits to protected branches with mandatory review trigger a build, unit and integration tests, static analysis, dependency and security scanning, then a versioned artifact. The same artifact is promoted through environments with deployment verification and an easy rollback. Secrets stay out of source control. I would also plan database migrations to be backward compatible, so the application and schema can change in separate, safe steps.
questions.revision: Reviewed commit, reproducible build, tests and scans, one versioned artifact promoted through environments, verified deploy, rollback ready. Secrets outside source; migrations backward compatible.
questions.detailed:
A CI/CD pipeline turns a code change into a verified, deployable artifact and moves it to production with as little manual risk as possible. Continuous integration proves the change is sound; continuous delivery or deployment moves it forward.

{{diagram:pipeline}}

## Stages and their purpose
```yaml
stages:
  - build        # reproducible, pinned dependencies
  - test         # unit and integration tests
  - analyse      # lint, static analysis, dependency and secret scanning
  - package      # one versioned, immutable artifact (image)
  - deploy-test  # automated deploy and smoke tests
  - approve      # optional gate for regulated environments
  - deploy-prod  # progressive rollout with health checks
  - verify       # post-deploy checks and alerts watched
```

## Design principles
- **Build once, promote the same artifact**: rebuilding per environment hides differences.
- **Fast feedback first**: cheap checks early, slower suites later or in parallel.
- **Protect the trunk**: branch protection, required reviews and passing checks before merge.
- **Secrets**: use a managed secret store or short-lived credentials; never commit them or print them in logs.
- **Infrastructure as code** so environments are consistent.
- **Rollback**: keep the previous artifact deployable; automate rollback triggers from health checks.
- **Database changes**: use expand-and-contract migrations (add, deploy code that handles both, then remove) so a rollback does not meet an incompatible schema.

## Trade-offs and mistakes
- Gates that are too slow or flaky push teams to bypass them; quarantine flaky tests.
- Manual approvals everywhere remove the speed benefit; reserve them for real risk.
- Treating the pipeline as unowned: it needs maintenance like any product.
- Testing only the happy path and having no post-deploy verification.

## Example (hypothetical)
A service pipeline builds an image tagged with the commit ID, runs tests and scans, deploys to a test environment, runs smoke tests, then rolls out to production gradually. If the error rate alarm fires, the previous image is redeployed automatically.

diagrams.title: CI/CD flow
diagrams.alt: A reviewed commit triggers build, then tests and scans, then packaging into a versioned artifact. The artifact is deployed to a test environment, verified, then released to production with monitoring and a rollback path.

followUps: How do you handle database migrations safely in a pipeline?
How do you manage secrets in CI/CD?
How would you deal with flaky tests blocking releases?
Continuous delivery versus continuous deployment: what is the difference?

questions.title: Docker versus Kubernetes: what is the difference and when do you need orchestration?
questions.quick: Docker packages an application with its dependencies into a container image and runs it consistently anywhere. Kubernetes orchestrates many containers across a cluster: scheduling, service discovery, scaling, self-healing and rolling updates. They solve different problems and are not alternatives. I would adopt Kubernetes only when the scale or complexity justifies the operational overhead. For a small application or a lean team, I would prefer managed container services such as ECS on Fargate, or serverless, and keep operations simple.
questions.revision: Docker packages and runs containers; Kubernetes orchestrates them across a cluster. Use Kubernetes only when orchestration needs justify the overhead; lean teams often do better with managed containers.
questions.detailed:
**Docker** is a toolset for building container images and running containers: an application plus its runtime and libraries in an isolated, portable unit. **Kubernetes** is a cluster orchestrator that decides where containers run, keeps the desired number alive, routes traffic to them and rolls out new versions.

## Different layers
| Question | Docker (image/runtime) | Kubernetes (orchestrator) |
|---|---|---|
| Main job | Package and run a container | Manage many containers across nodes |
| Scope | One host | A cluster of hosts |
| Scaling and healing | Manual or scripted | Declarative replicas, probes, rescheduling |
| Networking | Host-level ports and networks | Service discovery, ingress, network policies |
| Config and secrets | Environment or files | ConfigMaps and Secrets objects |

Kubernetes does not require Docker specifically; it runs containers through a standard runtime interface, and images built with Docker work.

## When orchestration pays off
- Many services owned by multiple teams needing a common platform.
- Need for portability across clouds or on-premises.
- Rich scheduling, custom controllers or ecosystem tooling.
- A platform team able to operate it.

## When it does not
- A handful of services and a small team: the cluster, upgrades, networking, RBAC and observability become the project.
- Managed alternatives (ECS with Fargate, App Runner-style services, or Lambda) remove most node and control-plane work. A managed Kubernetes service reduces but does not remove the burden.

## Common mistakes
- Treating Kubernetes as a goal, not a means.
- Running images as root, with no resource requests or limits, or with the latest tag.
- Putting stateful databases in the cluster without a clear operations plan.
- Skipping health probes, so the orchestrator cannot heal anything.

## Example (hypothetical)
A team with three internal APIs ships Docker images to ECS on Fargate. Two years later, with thirty services and a platform group, it evaluates managed Kubernetes for standard tooling and policy control.
followUps: What is the difference between an image and a container?
What are liveness and readiness probes for?
How would you decide between ECS and EKS?

questions.title: How do you monitor a production application?
questions.quick: I would combine metrics, structured logs and distributed traces, plus business-level indicators. I watch latency percentiles, error rate, throughput and saturation such as CPU, memory, queue depth and database health, and failures from dependencies. Alerts should be actionable and tied to service objectives, so they fire on user impact, not every blip. Correlation IDs let me follow a request across services. For enterprise workflows I would also track completion rates and failed business transactions, because a system can be technically up while the business process is failing.
questions.revision: Metrics, structured logs, traces and business indicators. Track latency percentiles, errors, throughput and saturation; alert on user impact against objectives; use correlation IDs across services.
questions.detailed:
Monitoring answers "is it working for users, and if not, where is it broken?". Observability is the property that lets you ask new questions about a system from its telemetry. Production monitoring uses several complementary signals.

## Signals
| Signal | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Metrics | Trends and alerting | Request rate, error rate, p95/p99 latency, CPU, queue depth |
| Logs | Event detail | Structured JSON with request ID, user-safe context, error cause |
| Traces | Request path across services | Which downstream call added 800 ms |
| Business metrics | Real outcomes | Orders completed, payments failed, jobs stuck |
| Synthetic checks | External view | A scripted login every minute |

A useful checklist is the "golden signals": latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Track percentiles, not just averages, since averages hide slow tails.

## Alerting
- Alert on **symptoms** (users see errors or slowness), and keep cause-based metrics for diagnosis dashboards.
- Tie alerts to **service level objectives**; burn-rate alerts reduce noise.
- Each alert needs an owner, a severity and a runbook link.

```yaml
# Illustrative alert idea, not tied to a specific tool
alert: HighErrorRate
condition: 5xx_ratio > 2% for 10 minutes
severity: page
runbook: link-to-runbook
```

## Practices
- Propagate a **correlation ID** through every service and include it in logs and traces.
- Keep logs structured and free of secrets and personal data.
- Monitor dependencies (database, queues, third-party APIs) and retries.
- Review dashboards and alert quality regularly; delete alerts nobody acts on.

## Common mistakes
- Alerting on CPU alone and missing real user failures.
- Unstructured logs that cannot be searched, or logs so verbose they cost more than they help.
- No business indicator, so a silent failure in a workflow goes unnoticed.
- Monitoring only the average.

## Example (hypothetical)
A claims-processing workflow shows healthy servers, but the "claims completed per hour" metric drops to zero. A trace reveals a downstream validation service timing out, and the alert fires on the business metric before users call.
followUps: What are SLIs, SLOs and error budgets?
How do you reduce alert fatigue?
What is the difference between monitoring and observability?

questions.title: Explain blue-green and canary deployments.
questions.quick: In blue-green I run two production environments: the live one and an identical new one. After validating the new one, I switch traffic over, and switching back is my rollback. In a canary release I route a small share of traffic to the new version and increase it as health signals stay good. Both reduce release risk. The hard parts are shared concerns: database compatibility, background workers, state changes and whether a rollback is truly safe after data has been written.
questions.revision: Blue-green swaps all traffic between two full environments; canary shifts traffic gradually on health signals. Both need backward-compatible data and a safe rollback.
questions.detailed:
Both strategies limit the blast radius of a bad release by avoiding an in-place, all-at-once update.

{{diagram:bg}}

## Blue-green
Two environments exist: **blue** (current) and **green** (new). Deploy and test green while blue serves users, then switch the router or load balancer to green. Rollback means pointing back to blue.

## Canary
Send a small percentage of real traffic (or specific users) to the new version, watch error rate and latency against the baseline, then step up (for example 5%, 25%, 100%) or abort automatically.

| Aspect | Blue-green | Canary |
|---|---|---|
| Traffic shift | All at once (or fast) | Gradual |
| Rollback speed | Very fast switch back | Fast, with limited users affected |
| Infrastructure cost | Duplicate environment during release | Small extra capacity |
| Real-traffic validation | Only before the switch | Continuous, on live traffic |
| Complexity | Environment parity | Traffic splitting and metric analysis |

## What can still go wrong
- **Database changes**: both versions may run against one schema at the same time. Use backward-compatible, expand-and-contract migrations. A destructive migration breaks rollback.
- **State and sessions**: users should not lose sessions or see inconsistent behaviour mid-rollout.
- **Background workers and queues**: old and new consumers may process the same messages with different logic.
- **Data written by the new version** may not be readable by the old one.
- **Weak health signals**: a canary only helps if you compare meaningful metrics.

## Mistakes
- Treating blue-green as safe without schema compatibility planning.
- Promoting a canary based on "no complaints" rather than metrics.
- Leaving the idle environment out of date or unmonitored.

## Example (hypothetical)
A checkout service releases a new pricing module to 5% of traffic. Error rate and latency match baseline for thirty minutes, so the share rises in steps. A rise in errors would trigger an automatic return to the previous version.

diagrams.title: Traffic routing during release
diagrams.alt: A router sends all traffic to the blue environment in blue-green, switching to green after validation. In a canary, the router sends a small share to the new version and the rest to the stable version, based on health metrics.

followUps: How would you roll back a release that included a database migration?
What metrics decide whether a canary is promoted?
How do feature flags relate to these strategies?

questions.title: What are RTO and RPO, and how do they shape design?
questions.quick: RTO, the recovery time objective, is the maximum acceptable time to restore a service after a disruption. RPO, the recovery point objective, is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time. Together they drive design: backup frequency, replication, failover architecture and how often we test recovery. I would agree the numbers with business stakeholders for each application based on criticality, because tighter targets cost more. A target that has never been tested in a recovery exercise is only an assumption.
questions.revision: RTO is how long you can be down; RPO is how much data, in time, you can lose. Agree them per application with the business; they dictate backup, replication and failover design.
questions.detailed:
**RTO** (recovery time objective) is the longest outage the business accepts before service is restored. **RPO** (recovery point objective) is the longest span of data the business accepts losing, measured backwards from the disruption.

If the last good copy of data is 15 minutes old at failure time, the data loss is 15 minutes. An RPO of 15 minutes means backups or replication must be at least that frequent. An RTO of one hour means the whole recovery process (detect, decide, restore, verify, redirect traffic) must fit in an hour.

## How targets map to strategy
| Strategy | Typical recovery speed | Typical cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Backup and restore | Hours | Lowest | Restore time grows with data size |
| Pilot light | Tens of minutes to hours | Low | Core data replicated; compute started on demand |
| Warm standby | Minutes | Medium | Scaled-down copy always running |
| Active-active | Seconds to minutes | Highest | Complex data consistency |

These are commonly cited disaster recovery patterns; actual times depend on your implementation.

## Setting the numbers
- Classify applications by business impact, then set targets per tier, not one number for everything.
- Express the cost of downtime and data loss so stakeholders can trade money against risk.
- Different components may differ: a payments database may need near-zero RPO while a reporting store tolerates a day.

## Common mistakes
- Confusing RTO/RPO with availability percentages or backup retention periods.
- Backing up without ever testing a restore.
- Ignoring dependencies, such as DNS, secrets, identity or third-party services, in the recovery plan.
- Assuming Multi-AZ equals disaster recovery; it covers a zone failure, not a Region failure or data corruption that replicates.
- Setting aggressive targets nobody has budgeted for.

## Example (hypothetical)
An order system is classified Tier 1 with RTO 30 minutes and RPO 5 minutes. The team uses continuous database replication to a second Region, infrastructure as code for the standby stack, and a quarterly failover exercise that measures real recovery time against the target.
followUps: What is the difference between high availability and disaster recovery?
How would you test that RTO and RPO are actually met?
Which DR pattern would you pick for a low-criticality internal tool?

questions.title: How would you investigate a sudden production outage?
questions.quick: I would first assess scope and business impact and make sure the right people know. Then I check alerts and recent changes such as deployments or configuration. I look at application and infrastructure metrics to decide whether the failure sits in the application, database, network or a dependency. My priority is to mitigate quickly through rollback, failover or traffic control, and only then dig for the root cause. Afterwards I run a blameless review, assign corrective actions with owners and add monitoring to catch it earlier.
questions.revision: Scope and impact, recent changes, narrow the failing layer, mitigate first (rollback, failover, throttle), then root cause, corrective actions with owners and better monitoring.
questions.detailed:
During an outage the goal is to **restore service first** and understand fully second. A calm, structured approach avoids random changes that make things worse.

{{diagram:incident}}

## Workflow
1. **Declare and coordinate**: name an incident lead, open a shared channel, keep a timeline, communicate status to stakeholders at a steady cadence.
2. **Assess impact**: who is affected, which journeys fail, how severe, is data at risk?
3. **Check what changed**: recent deployments, configuration, feature flags, certificate expiry, infrastructure or dependency changes. Most incidents follow a change.
4. **Narrow the layer**: use the golden signals. Is traffic arriving? Are errors from the app, the database, the network, or an external dependency? Compare to a known good baseline.
5. **Mitigate**: roll back the release, disable a flag, fail over, scale out, shed or throttle traffic, or restart a stuck component. Prefer reversible actions.
6. **Verify recovery** with user-facing metrics, not just green hosts.
7. **Root cause and follow-up** once stable.

## Triage table
| Symptom | First checks |
|---|---|
| Errors right after a release | Roll back, diff the change |
| High latency, CPU fine | Database locks, slow queries, dependency timeouts |
| Intermittent failures | One bad instance, connection pool exhaustion, DNS |
| Everything down | Network, load balancer health, certificates, cloud provider status |

## Post-incident
Hold a **blameless review**: timeline, contributing factors, what detection and mitigation worked, and concrete actions with owners and dates (alerts, tests, runbooks, safer rollouts).

## Common mistakes
- Debugging deeply while users are still down.
- Making several changes at once, so nothing is attributable.
- No clear lead, causing duplicated or conflicting actions.
- Declaring victory without confirming user-facing recovery.
- Writing a review that blames a person rather than fixing the system.

## Example (hypothetical)
Checkout errors spike ten minutes after a deployment. The lead rolls back, errors clear, and the review finds a new query without an index that exhausted database connections. Actions: query review step in the pipeline and a connection-saturation alert.

diagrams.title: Incident workflow
diagrams.alt: An alert leads to assessing impact, checking recent changes and narrowing the failing layer. The team mitigates, verifies recovery, and then holds a blameless review that produces corrective actions.

followUps: When would you roll back versus fix forward?
What belongs in a post-incident review?
How do you communicate with non-technical stakeholders during an outage?

questions.title: How do you optimize cloud costs without hurting reliability?
questions.quick: I would start with visibility: tagging, cost reports and knowing which workloads drive spend. Then I look for idle resources, overprovisioned compute, storage growth, database sizing, data transfer, log volume and forgotten environments. Typical actions are right-sizing, autoscaling, storage lifecycle policies and using managed services where they genuinely reduce cost or effort. I validate every change against latency, availability and recovery requirements, so I'm not optimising cost in isolation and cutting something that protects the business.
questions.revision: Get visibility first, then remove idle and oversized resources, add autoscaling and storage lifecycle rules, and review transfer and logging. Validate against performance, availability and recovery needs.
questions.detailed:
Cost optimisation means getting the required outcomes for the least waste, not simply spending less. Cutting a cost that protects availability or recovery usually creates a larger cost later.

## Step 1: make spend visible
- Enforce **tags** (team, environment, application) and use cost allocation reports and budgets with alerts.
- Identify the top few cost drivers; effort should follow money.

## Step 2: look for waste
| Area | What to check | Typical action |
|---|---|---|
| Compute | Low utilisation, oversized instances | Right-size, autoscale, schedule non-production shutdown |
| Pricing model | Steady baseline on on-demand pricing | Consider commitment-based discounts for stable load |
| Storage | Old snapshots, unattached volumes, cold data in hot tiers | Lifecycle policies, tiering, deletion rules |
| Database | Oversized instances, unused replicas | Right-size, review engine and storage settings |
| Data transfer | Cross-zone or cross-Region traffic, internet egress | Keep chatty services together, use a CDN, review architecture |
| Observability | Verbose logs, long retention | Sampling, retention tiers, log levels |
| Environments | Forgotten test stacks | Expiry tags and automated cleanup |

## Step 3: design for efficiency
Use managed services when they replace operational effort, serverless for spiky work and caching to cut repeated load. Reassess architecture decisions as usage changes.

## Guardrails
- Check performance, availability and recovery objectives before downsizing; a Multi-AZ database or a second Region is a deliberate cost.
- Make changes gradually with monitoring, and keep a rollback.
- Assign ownership so teams see their own costs.

## Common mistakes
- One-off cost clean-ups with no governance, so spend creeps back.
- Buying long commitments before usage is understood.
- Ignoring data transfer and logging until the bill arrives.
- Removing redundancy or backups to hit a number.

## Example (hypothetical)
A review finds test environments running around the clock, an object bucket with years of rarely read exports, and debug-level logs retained for a long period. The team schedules shutdowns, adds a lifecycle rule to cheaper storage and reduces log level and retention, saving money with no change to production resilience.
followUps: How do you decide between on-demand and committed pricing?
How would you cost-optimise a data-transfer-heavy workload?
How do you give teams accountability for their own cloud spend?
